did.abstract: The John Wolcott Papers document Wolcott's involvement in the revival of the historic Pinxter Festival, grassroots efforts to preserve the Pine Bush, and archaeological and historical research in Albany, New York.
did.physloc: The materials are located onsite in the department.

accessrestrict.head: Access
accessrestrict.p: Access to this record group is unrestricted.

acqinfo.head: Acquisition Information
acqinfo.p: John Wolcott first donated his materials to the M.E. Grenander Department of Special Collections and Archives in 2007, with additions in 2013.

appraisal.head: Appraisal
appraisal.p: Approximately two cubic feet of material that John Wolcott donated with his personal papers consisted of legal and administrative records of Save the Pine Bush. These were transferred to the Save the Pine Bush, Inc. collection. Similarly, approximately 0.5 cubic feet of material donated by Save the Pine Bush, Inc. was labeled "Papers from John Wolcott" and consisted of newspaper clippings that Wolcott collected about not only the Pine Bush, but archaeology, historic preservation, and environmental protection more broadly. These were transferred to Wolcott's personal papers.

arrangement.head: Arrangement of the Collection
arrangement.p: The collection is arranged chronologically. There are no series.

bioghist.head: Biographical Sketch
bioghist.p: John Wolcott was born on September 22, 1932, in the Albany, New York region. He was a lifelong community activist in the Capital Region, focusing on historic preservation and environmentalism. An article from the Albany Times Union describes him as "a passionate long-time defender of preserving the Pine Bush ecosystem, self-proclaimed Albany historian, and thorn in the side of developers and government officials for decades."

Wolcott served as chairman of the Pinxter Committee of Albany, which coordinated the annual Pinxter Festival, also referred to as Pinkster, Dutch for Pentecost, or Whitsuntide. During the colonial period, Pinxter celebrations were held throughout eastern New York in communities of Dutch origins. Africans played a major role in organizing Pinxter, adding African music and dance to the festivities. In 1811 the Common Council of the City of Albany passed a Whitsuntide Holiday law which banned the essential elements of the festival and, as a result, the festival died out. In 1972, Pinxter was revived in Albany and celebrated on Sundays during Tulip Fest in Washington Park with craft vendors and musicians. It was often advertised as an illegal festival. Wolcott wrote several letters asking for the 1811 law to be repealed. The Whitsuntide Holiday Law was repealed in 2011, two hundred years after it was enacted.

Wolcott was also actively involved in advocating for the preservation of the Albany Pine Bush beginning in the early 1970s. The Pine Bush is home to the largest inland pine barrens sand dunes in the United States, and to tens of thousands of species of flora and fauna, including the endangered Karner Blue Butterfly. Wolcott first became interested in the Pine Bush after visiting it in his early childhood. He was a founding member of the Pine Bush Ski Club, formed in 1977, and of Save the Pine Bush, Inc., established on February 6, 1978, to protest proposed development plans within the Pine Bush. Wolcott's involvement in Save the Pine Bush centered around conducting historical and archaeological research into the preserve, creating trail maps, and leading hikes and skiing trips through the Pine Bush. In 1999, Wolcott was involved in advocating for a hikers' underpass where Route 155 crosses over the New York State Thruway. In October 2025, the underpass was designated the John Wolcott Pine Bush Hikers' Underpass in his honor.

His research and advocacy extended beyond Pinxter Fest and the Pine Bush to include the preservation of historic structures across Albany and the broader Capital Region. In a 2023 interview with WAMC, former Albany city archaeologist Don Rittner recalled that "for so many years [Wolcott] would battle [Mayor] Corning over saving a lot of the historic buildings in downtown [Albany]...John was always going down to the Common Council chambers during public hearings, and basically reading the riot act." Some of Wolcott's notable contributions to local Dutch colonial history knowledge include pinpointing the location of the Fort Orange settlement and determining that the Van Ostrande-Radliff House at 48 Hudson Avenue actually dated to 1728, not 1759 as previously thought, making it the oldest extant structure in Albany.

Professionally, Wolcott was employed by the New York State Historic Trust as a member of the Fort Orange Excavation team from 1970-1971, and later by the Office of Real Property Tax Services, where he performed title searches into 17th, 18th, and 19th century deeds. He and his wife, Linda Becker, who also played an active role in Pinxter Fest planning and Pine Bush advocacy herself, were married for nearly 50 years. He passed away on August 17, 2023, at the age of 90.
For more information on Wolcott, see the website of Save the Pine Bush, Inc.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection documents Wolcott's involvement with the Pinxter Committee of Albany and Save the Pine Bush, Inc., as well as his general work in historical research, archaeology, and environmental protection within the Capital Region. Materials include event posters, flyers, and programs; research notes and materials; news clippings; correspondence, particularly with local legislators; copies of relevant laws and policies; photographs; and Wolcott's notebooks, notepads, and loose notes. Material of note relating to Pinxter Fest include an early souvenir Tulip Fest envelope, contact information for craft vendors, and a small collection of colonial Dutch recipes. Material of note relating to the Pine Bush include Wolcott's notes from the founding meeting, archaeological reports, petitions against commercial development, maps, and trail guides. Maps are attributed to the creators when that information is known. There are instances where Wolcott edited existing maps originally created by others. If the date of the edits is unknown, the date of the original map is given.

The collection is particularly strong in its documentation of ad-hoc and grassroots advocacy on behalf of the Pine Bush during the 1970s; Wolcott's dealings with the City of Albany, the Town of Guilderland, and the Town of Colonie; and Wolcott's research into the following local history topics: the Maquas Padt/King's Highway, the Isaac Truax tavern, Henry Rowe Schoolcraft, and the changes in land ownership within and around the Albany Pine Bush across time. Some files from the 1970s were listed as having belonged to Wolcott's friend and colleague, George Keleshian, who was the co-chairman of SUNY Albany's Environmental Decisions Commission, and these are noted in the folder titles. Many of Wolcott's personal papers documenting his research into the colonial Dutch heritage of the city of Albany were lost in a 2021 house fire.
